extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, probability, and inductive reasoning (e.g., philosophers, statisticians, scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for estimating probabilities, deciding when coincidences indicate causation, and extending empirical laws to adjacent cases; focused on the foundations of the doctrine of chances and induction. Useful for evaluating the legitimacy of probabilistic reasoning and causal inference in scientific and everyday contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's definition of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is the ratio of the number of cases favorable to an event to the number of all possible cases; reduce events to a set of equally possible cases and take the fraction favorable as the measure of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace: 'The theory of chances consists in reducing all events of the same kind to a certain number of cases equally possible... The ratio of that number to the number of all the possible cases is the measure of the probability.' The equally-possible assumption is operationalized by symmetry or by knowledge of frequencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for Laplacian calculation of chances
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things are required for the standard calculation of chances: (1) among several events some one, and only one, must certainly happen; (2) we must have no reason to expect any one of them rather than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these prerequisites do not hold, the simple ratio-of-cases calculus is not justified. Equal probability often needs support from experience (observed frequencies) or deductive symmetry (mechanical reasons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal probability must be justified by experience or symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: To call two events equally probable requires either observed equal frequency in many trials or deductive reasons (symmetry/mechanics) supporting equal incidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: coin tosses are treated as equally probable because experience or mechanical symmetry of the coin supports that belief; without such support, assuming equal chance is unfounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as degree of belief contingent on evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is not a property of the event but the degree of ground we (or someone) have for expecting the event; probabilities differ between persons and can change with new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one's estimate that an unfamiliar person will die within a year changes drastically if told the person is in the last stage of consumption. Thus probabilities are subjective in the sense of being evidence-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning under ignorance — acting 'as if' equal frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When all we know is that possible mutually exclusive contingencies exist and we have no reason to prefer any, we may rationally act as if they were equally likely (indifference principle), producing numerically appreciable grounds for conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with three colors of balls and no information on proportions, one may rationally bet on 'not white' at 2:1 against white because the other two colors together are twice as probable as one alone. But this is only a fallback when better knowledge is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer specific experience or causal knowledge over minimal-case reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, probabilities should be estimated from specific empirical frequencies or, preferably, from knowledge of the causes that produce the effects rather than from bare counting of logical possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight improvement in observational data or causal understanding improves probability estimates more than elaborate application of calculus to poor data. Example: ball size affects draw probability even if counts are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is the foundation of empirical probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation of chances grounded on observed frequencies is an induction: probability equals the ascertained proportion between the number of cases in which the event occurs and the total number of cases of that description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actuarial tables, hospital returns, and registers illustrate that many practical probabilities (mortality, recovery rates, ship loss) are derived from observed frequencies rather than from direct knowledge of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal (cause-based) probabilities are superior to raw frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, deduce probabilities from knowledge of the causes on which the occurrence depends, because such cause-based estimates are of a 'higher order' and will correct or confirm mere empirical ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a box with nine black and one white ball, the chance of drawing a black is because the local conditions (nine places) are more favorable; if balls differ in size the causal condition (size) alters probability despite counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's Sixth Principle (probability of causes given effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an observed effect and several possible causes, the probability that the effect was produced by any one cause is proportional to the antecedent probability of that cause multiplied by the probability that the cause, if present, would produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental rule for 'ascending from events to causes' (a Bayes-like rule). It requires assessment of antecedent (prior) probabilities and the likelihoods (probability of effect given the cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicative rule for comparing competing causes (three cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing two causes A and B for effect M, the relative probability that A caused M is the product of (antecedent probability of A) and (probability A would produce M), and similarly for B; special cases illustrate simple ratios: (I) equal capacities to produce M but different antecedent frequencies; (II) equal antecedent frequencies but different production rates; (III) differing in both respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill demonstrates with numerical examples (e.g., A twice as frequent as B, or A produces M 2/3 times while B 1/3) that the posterior odds equal the product of prior odds and likelihood ratio; work through counts to derive fractions like 4/7 and 3/7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing chance coincidences from causal laws by excess over expected chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the observed number of coincidences to the average number expected from chance alone: if the excess over the chance-average is so large that such a deviation would be extremely uncommon by accident, we have reason to infer causation and accept an empirical law (subject to further correction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses the doctrine of chances to evaluate whether a pattern is unlikely under accidental conjunctions. Practical decisions often rely on ability to repeat the experiment and on how rapidly the accidental probability diminishes with repeated concordant instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations when the alternative hypothesis (unknown law) has unknown antecedent probability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the coincidences could only be explained by an as-yet-undiscovered law, the antecedent probability of that hypothesis is unknowable and cannot be numerically compared to the accidental hypothesis; precise numerical estimation then fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases one can only conclude empirically if the observed excess is very unlikely under chance; one cannot compute exact posterior odds because the prior probability of 'an unknown law' is not assessable. Repetition and consideration of plausible known causes remain essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws have inferior generality and are conditional on collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (uniformities of co-existence/sequence between effects) are less general and less certain than the ultimate laws from which they derive; they hold only where the same collocation of primeval causes obtains and may fail if collocations vary or counteracting causes intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: day followed by night derives from Earth's rotation and sun illumination; if collocations change (e.g., different illuminating body, rotation halted), the derivative law (alternation of day/night) need not hold even though the ultimate law about causes remains true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are admissible only within observed conditions of time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical (derivative) laws are only reliably extendable within the specific conditions of collocation (time/place) confirmed by observation; extrapolation beyond those conditions is precarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence, when applying observed regularities to adjacent or future cases, verify that the same combination of relevant causes and absence of counteracting influences is plausibly preserved; otherwise the derivative law may not apply.
